For	 many	 small	 and	 remote	 Tribes	 in	 Alaska,
economies	of	scale	make	it	extremely	 difficult	 to	provide
all	 government 	 services	 to	 which 	 their	 citizens	 are
entitled.	 Therefore,	 these	 Tribes	 have	 chosen	 to	 join
together	 to	 form	 self-governing	 Tribal	 consortia	 that
serve	 multiple	 communities	 across	 their	 respective
regions.	 These	 consortia	 are	 generally 	 formed	 around
cultural, historical, regional, and ecological bonds, and
allow	Tribes	to	pool	their	resources	and	take	advantage	of
efficiencies	of	scale	when	providing 	government	services
for	their	 member	Tribes.	 Each	Amicus thus represents
Tribal 	 governments	 coming 	 together	 to	 exercise 	 selfdetermination	to	meet	the	needs	of	their	citizens,	including
through	the	operation	of	health	care	facilities,	support	for
tribal	administration,	and	the	deployment	of	public	safety
and	social	service	programs	“appropriate	to	their	diverse
demographic, 	 geographic, 	 economic[,]	 and	 institutional
needs.” S. Rep. No. 100-274 (Dec. 21, 1987), as reprinted
in	 1988	 U.S.C.C.A.N.	 2620,	 2625	 (Select	 Committee	 on
Indian	 Affairs	 Report).	Tribal	 consortia	 also	 serve	 as	 a
unified	advocacy	voice	for	their	member	Tribes,	providing
individual 	 Tribes	 with 	 the	 ability 	 to	 engage 	 in	 policy
discussions 	 without 	 incurring 	 the	 heavy 	 financial 	 and
administrative	 burden	 of	 each	 doing	 it	 by	 themselves.
Alaska’s	 geography	 demands	 creative	 solutions,	 and
Tribal 	consortia 	are	a	practical, 	efficient	model	of	Tribal
self-governance.
Amici and 	 the 	 Tribal	 governments	 they	 serve
understand	 firsthand	 the	 harms	 that	 the	 unlawful
importation	 of	 alcohol	 brings	 to	 their	 communities.
Accordingly,	 the	 majority	 of	 the	 Tribal	 governments
comprising	Amici are	 located	 in	 communities	 that	 have
elected	 to	 adopt	 some	form	 of	the	 local	 option	 available

SUMMARY OF ARGUMENT
This	case	cannot	be	considered	outside	of	its	geographic
context.	A laska	is	the	largest	state	by	land	mass	by	a	w ide
margin— over	two	times	as	large	as	the	next	largest	state
(Texas)—	but	is	the	least	densely	populated	state.3 Nearly
half	 the	 population	 lives	 in	 the	 State’s	 urban	 center	 in
southcentral	Alaska, 	while	17%	of	Alaskans 	live	in	rural
Alaska—remote	 communities	 with	 under	 2,500	 people,
many	with	just	a	few	hundred	residents	or	less.	Id. Alcohol
has	been	a	primary	 factor	 in	an	overwhelming	 majority
of	 incidents	 of	 interpersonal	 violence	 and	 accidental
injury	in	rural	Alaska.	 The	remote	and	isolated	nature	of
rural	 Alaska,	 coupled	with	 decades	 of	State	 neglect	and
centralization	 of	power	and	services	 in	urban	areas,	 has
left	 rural	 Alaska	 Native	communities	 without	 adequate
resources	 to	provide	 for	the	comprehensive	government
services	needed	to	address	the	harms	of	alcohol,	or	even
the	emergency	services	 needed	to	respond	to	an	incident
involving a single intoxicated person. As a result, alcohol’s
well-documented	personal	and	social	harms	are	worsened
in	communities—like	 many	served	 by	Amici—that	lack

full-time,	 armed	 law	enforcement	and	robust	health	and
social services.
It is against this backdrop that the Alaska Legislature
enacted	the	State’s	local	option	law,	empowering	Alaskan
communities	to	ban	or	place	limitations	on	the	importation,
sale,	and	possession	of	alcohol,	w ith	penalties	sufficient	to
serve as a realistic deterrent. As the Alaska Legislature
understood,	once	alcohol	has	arrived	in	a	small	community
with	 no	formal	 law	 enforcement	 and	 limited	 emergency
response	services,	 it	is	simply	too	late	to	stop	the	harms
it	 might	 cause.	 In	 enacting	 local	 option	 and	 the	 related
forfeiture	 statutes,	 the	 Alaska	 Legislature	 prioritized
public	 safety	 and	 local	 control,	 and	 provided	 a	 tool	 for
small,	 predominantly	 Alaska	 Native	 communities	 to
protect	themselves.
In contrast, Petitioner ignores the uniquely Alaskan
context	 for	 the	 local	 option	 statutes,	 misrepresents	 the
facts	of	the	case,	and	prioritizes 	the	value	of	his	personal
property 	 over 	 the 	 well-being 	 of	 the 	 Alaska	 Native
communities	 from	 which	 he	 profited.	 Petitioner	 frames
his	crime	as	minor	and	the	punishment	as	excessive—“a
Cessna	for	a	six-pack,”	in	his	telling. 	Pet.	Br.	35.	Y et	the
established	 facts	 of	the	case	show	that	Petitioner	nearly
transported nine gallons of	alcohol	to	a	village	 that	had
banned	 alcohol	 entirely.	 Furthermore, 	 the	 tremendous
personal	 and	social	 harms	 caused	 by	alcohol	in	Alaskan
communities	are	not	consequences	in	the	“abstract,”	Pet.
Br.	37;	they	are	well	documented	and	are	the	foreseeable
consequences	 of	 Petitioner’s	 actions	 had	 he	 not	 gotten
caught.	 These	 well-established	 harms	 put	 the	 gravity
analysis into clearer perspective and underscore the
reasonableness	of	the	forfeiture	here.	Indeed,	the	central

6
question	in	this	 case	is	whether	the	seizure	 of	a	piece	of
personal	property—even	an	expensive	one—is	reasonable
to avert the catastrophic consequences that the Alaska
Legislature	 recognized	 might	unfold	from	bringing	 any
amount	of	alcohol	into	an	isolated	community,	against	the
community’s	explicit	w ishes.	The	framing	is	not	“a	Cessna

III.	Local	 Option	 Laws	 are	 Effective	 and	 One	 of	 the
Few	Resources	 that	 Rural	 Communities	 Have	to
Combat	the	Specific	Harms	of	Alcohol.
Against	 the	backdrop	 of	the	challenges	 facing	 rural
Alaska, 	the	local	option	laws	are	one	of	the	few	available
tools	for	local	communities	to	protect	public	safety	within

23
their	 communities.	 While	 more	 remains	 to	 be	 done	 to
empower	 rural	 Alaska	 communities	 with	 the	 authority
and	resources	to	adequately	provide	for	their	own	public
safety,	 the	 Alaska	 Legislature’s	 establishment	 of	 the
State’s	local	option	law	in	1980	restored	to	remote	villages
an	important	tool—if	adopted	by	a	majority	of	the	voters
in	 the	 community—to	 control	 whether	 and	 how	 alcohol
is	imported	 into	their	 communities.	 See Resp’t Br. 7–12.
More	 specifically,	 local 	 option 	 allows 	 a	 community 	 to
vote	 to	 place	 various	 restrictions	 on	 the	 importation,
possession,	 and	sale	of	alcohol.	Communities	 can	choose
to	be	fully	 “dry,”	meaning	 that	alcohol	is	entirely	 illegal
within	 the	community.	Alaska	 Stat.	 §	04.11.491(b)(4).	Or
a	 community	 can	 elect	 to	 allow	 for	 the	 possession	 and
importation	 of	alcohol,	while	 prohibiting	 its	sale.	Alaska
Stat.	§	04.11.491(b)(1).	Regardless	of	the	particular 	option
adopted 	 by	 a	 community,	 the	 adoption 	 of	 local 	 option
reflects	 a	 key	 exercise	 of	 local	 control	 that	 is	 vital	 to
rural	A laska.	Over	100	communities	across	the	state	have
demonstrated	 the	importance	 of	this	 tool	by	opting	 into
the	system	and	banning	alcohol	either	partially	or	entirely.
See Schedule of Local Option Communities .
The	forfeiture	law	challenged	 here	was	unanimously
adopted	by	the	Alaska	 Legislature	 in	the	spring	of	2004
with	the	goal	of	creating	 additional	 deterrence	 for	those
contemplating 	 bootlegging	 into	 dry	 communities.	 2004
Alaska	 Sess.	 Laws,	 ch.	 124,	 §11;	 2004	 Alaska	 House
Journal 4175; 2004 Alaska Senate Journal 3647; Resp’t
Br.	11.	Residents	of	Beaver,	the	community	at	issue	here,
voted	 to	 enter	 local	 option	 soon	 after.	 See Schedule of
Local Option Communities (noting that Beaver’s local
option	became	effective	on	August	1,	2004).

are	safer	places”	with	“fewer	assaults	and	fewer	injuries”

CONCLUSION
Here,	 the	 law	 accomplished	 precisely	 what	 was
intended by both the Alaska Legislature and the local
community:	 it	 stopped	 a	 pilot	 from	 bringing	 72	 beers,
amounting	to	nine	gallons	of	alcohol,	into	a	remote	A laska
village	 that,	 for	more	 than	 twenty	 years,	 has	 exercised
its	 option	 under	 state	 law	 to	 ban	 alcohol.	 Resp’t	 Br.	44
(citing	 R.686;	 App.159a).	 It	 is	 of	 no	 matter	 that	 he	 got
caught	before	his	 contraband	 could	 be	delivered	 or	that
he	 did	 not	 plan	 to	 watch	 anyone	 consume	 the	 alcohol.
Failing	to	enforce	the	associated	 statutory	penalties—of
which	Petitioner	acknowledges	he	was	aware—would	only
embolden	others	to	flout	the	law	and	bring	 more	alcohol
into	communities	that	voted	for	precisely	the	opposite.
As	 the	 Alaska	 Supreme	 Court 	 understood,	 even	 a
single	 six-pack	 of	 beer	 (not	 to	 mention	 the	 72	 cans	 of
